explain.title: A suspended magnet points north–south
explain.body: If a bar magnet is suspended horizontally through a string and allowed to come to rest, it will point in north-south direction. The end of the magnet that points north is called the north magnetic pole (N) and the end that points south is the south magnetic pole (S).

explain.title: How poles interact
explain.body: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Two north poles repel; two south poles repel; a north pole and a south pole attract.

explain.title: How to identify a magnet
explain.body: If the same end of an unknown object is attracted by both ends of a suspended magnet, it is a magnetic material. If it is repelled by the other end, it is a magnet. The repulsion between the like poles is a real test to identify a magnet.

explain.title: A magnet always has two poles
explain.body: Breaking a bar magnet does not give separate north and south poles. Each piece will have its two poles, i.e., N-pole and S-pole. Even if a magnet is divided into thousands pieces, each piece will be a complete magnet with its N, and S-poles.

modelAnswer: Yes, a magnetic field can give rise to an electric current.

The magnetic field through the coil changes and an emf is induced between the ends of the coil.

solution: Permanent magnets are essential parts of D.C. motors, A.C. and D.C. electric generators.

explain.body: An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet. The current in the coil produces a magnetic field that magnetizes the iron.

writtenQuestions.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with reference to the domain theory.

In diamagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields add up to zero, so each atom has no resultant field.

explain.title: Electrons can produce magnetism
explain.body: An electron revolves about the nucleus and also spins about an axis through it. Both motions give rise to a magnetic field. If the fields do not cancel, the atom behaves like a tiny magnet called a magnetic dipole.

explain.title: Paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials
explain.body: In paramagnetic materials, electron fields support one another, so atoms behave like tiny magnets; aluminium and lithium are examples. In diamagnetic materials, orbital and spin fields add up to zero; copper, bismuth and water are examples.

explain.title: Ferromagnetic materials contain domains
explain.body: Large groups of neighbouring atoms in ferromagnetic materials have electron spins naturally aligned parallel. Each domain is a highly magnetized region of about 0.1 mm size and acts as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.

explain.title: Alignment magnetizes iron
explain.body: Domains in unmagnetized iron point randomly, so their fields cancel. An external field makes suitably oriented domains grow and causes other domains to rotate towards the field. The iron then acts like a magnet.

explain.title: Soft iron and steel behave differently
explain.body: Soft-iron domains are easily oriented and return to random positions when the field is removed, which is useful in electromagnets and transformers. Steel is harder to align but retains its alignment, so it is used for permanent magnets.

mistakes: Do not say that a domain is a single electron; it is a region containing a large group of atoms.
Do not confuse a magnetic dipole (an atom with a resultant magnetic field) with a magnetic domain (a highly magnetized region in a ferromagnetic material).
Do not say that domains in unmagnetized iron are absent; they are present but randomly oriented.
Do not swap the behaviours of soft iron and steel: soft iron readily loses alignment, while steel retains it.
Do not describe diamagnetic atoms as having a resultant magnetic field; their orbital and spin fields add up to zero.

example.question: Describe how a varying sound or picture signal is recorded on a magnetic tape.

explain.title: What magnetic recording does
explain.body: Your textbook says, “Electromagnets have widely used in recording technology of sound, video and data in the form of electrical signals through magnetization of a magnetic material.” In simple terms, electrical signals create changing magnetism in a material so the information can be stored.

explain.title: How tape recording works
explain.body: “Induced magnetism is used in the process of magnetic tape recording.” The recording head is a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core. Varying currents make it an electromagnet, and its fringe field magnetises the coating on the moving tape.

explain.title: How information stays on tape
explain.body: “This induced magnetism is retained when the tape leaves the vicinity of the recording head.” During playback, the reverse process changes the varying induced magnetism into varying current, which is converted into sound or picture.

explain.title: How a hard disk records data
explain.body: A hard disk is a circular flat plate coated on both sides with iron oxide. Its small magnetic head writes a binary digit (1 or 0) by magnetising tiny spots in different directions, and reads the digit by detecting the direction of magnetisation.

explain.title: Why disks are useful
explain.body: A disk unit can read or write a recording instantly. Locating desired information on tape may take many minutes.

explain.title: Protecting electronic devices

Do not mix up the tape’s plastic backing with its magnetic coating; the coating records the information.

explain.title: How soft iron shields a device

explain.title: Other uses of soft iron

explain.title: Temporary and permanent magnets
explain.body: A temporary magnet loses most of its magnetism when the magnetising field is removed. A permanent magnet retains its magnetism.

explain.title: Magnetic fields and field lines
explain.body: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic effects can be detected. Magnetic lines of force represent the field's direction and shape. Outside a magnet, they go from north to south. Lines close together show a strong field; lines far apart show a weak field.

explain.title: Making and storing magnets
explain.body: Stroking is a common way to magnetise a material. A current-carrying solenoid also produces a magnetic field. Keepers made of soft iron are placed across the poles when magnets are stored.

explain.title: Magnetic materials and domains
explain.body: Magnetic domains are tiny regions in which atomic magnets are aligned in the same direction. Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted, diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled, and ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted.

explain.title: Electromagnets and induction
explain.body: An electromagnet uses current in a coil to produce a magnetic field and can be switched on or off. A changing magnetic field can also induce electric current, such as when a magnet moves relative to a coil.

explain.title: Magnets in devices
explain.body: Permanent magnets are used in devices such as loudspeakers. Electromagnets are useful in electric cranes and circuit breakers because their magnetic effect can be controlled by switching the current.

notes.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
notes.answer: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Brass, copper, wood, glass and plastic are non-magnetic materials.
notes.explanation: A magnet can attract some materials without touching them. Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials; brass, copper, wood, glass and plastic are non-magnetic materials. To tell whether an object is itself a magnet or only a magnetic material, test it with a known magnet: repulsion shows that the object is a magnet.
notes.simple: A magnet pulls some materials, such as iron, towards it. It does not pull materials such as wood or plastic.
examples: A paper clip made of iron is attracted to a magnet.
A plastic comb is not attracted to a magnet.
steps: Bring a known magnet close to the object.
If the object repels the magnet, the object is a magnet.
If the object is attracted but does not repel, it is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
notes.checkQuestion: What does repulsion by a known magnet tell you about an object?
notes.checkAnswer: An object that repels a known magnet is a magnet. An object that is only attracted is a magnetic material, not a magnet.

notes.title: Properties of Magnets
notes.answer: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.
notes.explanation: A magnet points north–south when freely suspended. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Attraction alone cannot prove that an object is a magnet: it may be a magnetic material. Repulsion by one pole of a suspended magnet is the real test.
notes.simple: Attraction does not prove an object is a magnet. Repulsion does.
examples: Bring an unknown object near the north pole of a suspended magnet. If it is attracted, it might be a south pole or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end near the south pole. If it is repelled, the object is a magnet; if it is attracted again, it is a magnetic material.
steps: Bring one end of the object near a pole of a suspended magnet.
If it is attracted, test the same end against the other pole.
If attracted by both poles, the object is a magnetic material.
If repelled by the other pole, the object is a magnet.

notes.title: Induced Magnetism
notes.answer: The S-pole induces an N-pole at the nail’s near end and an S-pole at its far end. The induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.
notes.explanation: A magnet can make a nearby piece of iron or steel act like a magnet. The end nearest the magnet gets the opposite pole, and the far end gets the other pole. When the true magnet is removed, the induced magnetism vanishes.
notes.simple: A magnet can make an iron nail act like a magnet for a while. Take the magnet away, and the nail loses this induced magnetism.
examples: Touch the head of an iron nail to the S-pole of a bar magnet: the nail’s near end becomes N and its far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet: the nail’s induced magnetism vanishes.
steps: Place the head of an iron nail against a pole of a bar magnet.
Bring a compass near the pointed end of the nail to check that the nail acts like a magnet.
For an S-pole touching the nail, the near end becomes N and the far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet and check the nail again; the induced magnetism vanishes.
notes.checkQuestion: If the S-pole of a bar magnet touches the head of an iron nail, which pole is induced at the nail’s near end?
notes.checkAnswer: The nail has induced magnetism; its near end becomes N and its far end becomes S, and the magnetism vanishes when the bar magnet is removed.

notes.title: Temporary and Permanent Magnets
notes.answer: The chain immediately collapses because the magnetism induced in the iron nails is temporary.
notes.explanation: A temporary magnet acts as a magnet while it is in a magnetic field, but loses its magnetism when that field disappears. A permanent magnet keeps its magnetic properties. Soft iron is commonly used for temporary magnets; steel and special alloys can be used for permanent magnets.
notes.simple: Temporary means the magnetism does not last once the outside magnetic field is gone. Permanent means the magnetism remains.
examples: An iron nail attracted to a magnet can temporarily attract another nail.
Cobalt, alnico and ferrite are examples of materials used for permanent magnets.
steps: Bring an iron nail into contact with a bar magnet.
The nail becomes a temporary magnet and can attract another iron nail.
Remove the chain from the bar magnet.
The iron-nail chain immediately collapses, showing that its induced magnetism was temporary.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to a chain of iron nails when it is pulled away from the bar magnet?
notes.checkAnswer: Temporary magnets lose their magnetic properties when the magnetic field vanishes; permanent magnets retain their magnetic properties.

notes.title: Magnetic Fields Around Magnets
notes.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where another magnetic object experiences a force.
notes.explanation: A magnetic field describes the region around a magnet where another magnetic object can feel a force. Magnetic lines of force show the field’s pattern and direction. Lines close together mean a stronger field; lines farther apart mean a weaker field.
notes.simple: A magnet affects magnetic objects around it, even when they are not touching it. The space where this effect happens is its magnetic field.
examples: A compass needle placed near a magnet turns because it experiences a magnetic force.
In a horseshoe magnet, the field is almost uniform in the gap between its poles, except near the edges.
steps: Look at the pattern of magnetic lines of force around a magnet.
Use the N-pole of a compass needle to find the field direction at a point.
Compare the spacing of the lines: closer lines show a stronger field.
Remember that fields of nearby magnets combine; they can cancel at a neutral point.
notes.checkQuestion: Where is a magnetic field stronger: where its lines are close together or far apart?
notes.checkAnswer: Magnetic field strength is greater where the magnetic lines of force are closer together.

notes.title: Uses of Permanent Magnets
notes.answer: Permanent magnets are used in generators and loudspeakers, as well as in door catchers, refrigerator door strips, flourmills, medical tools for removing iron splinters, and resetting the pointer in a maximum and minimum thermometer.
notes.explanation: Permanent magnets are used in devices and everyday tasks. In an A.C. generator, a rotating coil in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet produces an induced emf. In a loudspeaker, a changing current in the voice coil interacts with the magnet’s field, making the cone vibrate and produce sound.
notes.simple: A permanent magnet can help make electricity in a generator or help make sound in a loudspeaker.
examples: A.C. generator: a coil rotates between the poles of a permanent magnet.
Loudspeaker: the voice coil and attached cone move back and forth.
steps: In an A.C. generator, rotate a coil between the poles of a permanent magnet.
The magnetic field through the coil changes.
An emf is induced between the ends of the coil.
When the ends are connected to an external circuit, alternating current flows.
notes.checkQuestion: What produces the induced emf in an A.C. generator?
notes.checkAnswer: The changing magnetic field through the rotating coil induces an emf.

notes.title: Electromagnets: magnets made by current
notes.answer: The nail or rod becomes a magnet when electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.
notes.explanation: An electromagnet is made when electric current passes through a coil around an iron object. It acts as a magnet while current flows. Electromagnets are useful because their magnetism can be switched on and off.
notes.simple: A coil carrying current can make an iron nail magnetic. Turn off the current and the nail stops acting as a magnet.
examples: An iron nail inside a current-carrying coil can attract paper clips.
A scrapyard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift iron and steel, then releases them when the current is switched off.
steps: Wind a covered copper wire around an iron nail to make a coil.
Connect the coil to a battery through a switch.
Switch on the current: the nail becomes a magnet and can attract clips.
Switch off the current: the nail no longer remains a magnet.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens in a circuit breaker when the current becomes excessive?
notes.checkAnswer: A circuit breaker uses an electromagnet to attract an armature. If the current is excessive, the armature detaches from the copper strip and breaks the circuit.

notes.title: How magnetic domains make iron magnetic
notes.answer: The domains become more aligned with the external field, and the iron becomes magnetized.
notes.explanation: A magnetic domain is a small region in a ferromagnetic material where many neighbouring atoms act together like a tiny magnet. In unmagnetized iron, domains point in different directions. An external magnetic field makes more domains point in the same direction, so the iron becomes magnetized.
notes.simple: Imagine many tiny magnets inside iron. If they point in different directions, their effects cancel. If they turn to point mostly the same way, the iron acts like a magnet.
examples: Iron can be magnetized because it contains magnetic domains that can align.
Copper does not form magnetic domains, so magnetism cannot be induced into it in the way it can in iron.
steps: In unmagnetized iron, domains point in different directions.
An external magnetic field makes domains parallel or nearly parallel to it grow.
Other domains rotate towards the direction of the external field.
The iron becomes magnetized and has its own north and south poles.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the domains in an unmagnetized piece of iron when an external magnetic field is applied?
notes.checkAnswer: Domains whose magnetism is parallel or nearly parallel to the external field grow, and other domains rotate towards the field.

notes.title: Magnetising and demagnetising magnets
notes.answer: Steel can be magnetised by single-touch or double-touch stroking, or by placing it in a solenoid carrying direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by strong heating, hammering, or slowly withdrawing it from an A.C. solenoid.
notes.explanation: A steel bar can be magnetised by stroking it with a permanent magnet or by placing it inside a solenoid carrying direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by strong heating, hammering, or slowly moving it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.
notes.simple: Magnetising lines up the magnetic domains in a steel bar. Heating or hammering disturbs their alignment; A.C. in a solenoid can also demagnetise a magnet as it is slowly withdrawn.
examples: In single-touch stroking, stroke the bar several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the end of each stroke.
To demagnetise a magnet using A.C., place it inside a long solenoid carrying alternating current and move it out slowly.
steps: For single-touch, stroke the steel bar from one end to the other several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the far end.
For double-touch, stroke outwards from the centre using the unlike poles of two magnets at the same time.
For solenoid magnetisation, put the steel bar inside the solenoid and pass direct current through it; use the right-hand grip rule to identify its poles.
To demagnetise a magnet, heat it strongly, hammer it, or slowly move it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.
notes.checkQuestion: How do you find which end of a steel bar is its N-pole when it is inside a current-carrying solenoid?
notes.checkAnswer: Use the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers in the direction of current in the solenoid; the thumb points towards the bar's N-pole end.

notes.title: How magnets store sound, video and data
notes.answer: Magnetic recording stores information as magnetism in a tape’s coating or in tiny spots on a disk.
notes.explanation: The recording head acts as an electromagnet. In tape recording, its fringe field magnetises the moving tape’s coating. In a hard disk, a small magnetic head writes and reads information by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
notes.simple: The head changes electrical signals into magnetism on a tape or disk. Later, the stored magnetism can be read back.
examples: A tape stores sound or picture as varying magnetism in its magnetic coating.
A hard disk stores binary digits as magnetised spots.
steps: Varying currents reach the coil in the recording head.
The coil and iron core form an electromagnet.
The fringe field passes through the magnetic coating on the moving tape and induces magnetism.
The tape retains this induced magnetism after it leaves the head.
A hard disk head writes and reads binary digits by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
notes.checkQuestion: What part of the magnetic field magnetises the coating on a moving tape?
notes.checkAnswer: The fringe field penetrates the magnetic coating and induces magnetism in it.

notes.title: Soft Iron as a Magnetic Shield
notes.answer: A soft iron casing shields a sensitive magnetic device because magnetic flux is established in the soft iron rather than in the device.
notes.explanation: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability, so magnetic flux passes through it more easily than through air. A soft iron casing around a sensitive magnetic device provides an easier path for the flux, so the device is shielded from the external magnetic field.
notes.simple: Soft iron gives magnetic field lines an easier path than air. A soft iron cover can therefore keep much of the external magnetic field away from a sensitive device.
examples: A sensitive magnetic device can be protected by enclosing it in a soft iron casing.
A soft iron core in an electromagnet is easily magnetised when current flows and quickly loses its magnetism when the current stops.
steps: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability.
Its permeability is higher than that of air.
Magnetic flux is established in the soft iron casing rather than the sensitive device.
The device is therefore shielded from the external magnetic field.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does a soft iron casing shield a sensitive magnetic device?
notes.checkAnswer: The magnetic flux is established in the soft iron casing rather than in the device, shielding the device from the external magnetic field.

notes.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where magnetic effects can be observed.

A line that always points towards the south pole of Earth
rationales: This is incorrect because the lines describe the field pattern around the magnet, not only a path inside it.
This is correct because a compass needle moves along the magnetic lines of force.
This is incorrect because iron filings arrange themselves to show the field pattern.
This is incorrect because the direction depends on the magnetic field at the point, not always on Earth’s south pole.

quiz.stem: How is the direction of the magnetic field at a point identified?
options: By the direction of the compass needle’s N-pole
By the direction of the compass needle’s S-pole
By the colour of the magnet
By the size of the compass
rationales: This is correct because the field direction is the direction indicated by the compass needle’s N-pole.
This is incorrect because the textbook defines the direction using the N-pole.
This is incorrect because magnet colour does not identify field direction.
This is incorrect because compass size does not identify field direction.

quiz.stem: What spacing of magnetic lines indicates a stronger magnetic field?
options: The lines are closer together
The lines are farther apart
There are no lines around the poles
The lines form a straight line
rationales: This is correct because closer field lines indicate a stronger magnetic field.
This is incorrect because widely spaced lines indicate a weaker field.
This is incorrect because the field is particularly strong near the poles, where lines are close together.
This is incorrect because line spacing, not straightness, indicates relative field strength.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly describes the magnetic field around a bar magnet?
options: They spread out into separate straight rays
They go around a magnet in space, although a diagram may show only one plane
They exist only between the two poles
They stop at the edge of the paper
rationales: This is incorrect because magnetic field lines are not described as separate straight rays.
This is correct because the field extends all around the magnet, while a drawing may show only one plane.
This is incorrect because the magnetic field is not limited to the space between the poles.
This is incorrect because the edge of a drawing does not stop the real magnetic field.

quiz.stem: What is meant by a neutral point between two magnets?
options: The fields of the two magnets cancel at that point
The magnet has no poles at that point
The compass has stopped working
The field is strongest at that point
rationales: This is correct because a neutral point is where the field due to one magnet cancels the field due to the other.
This is incorrect because the neutral point does not mean the magnets lack poles.
This is incorrect because a neutral point is explained by cancellation of fields, not compass failure.
This is incorrect because cancellation means the resultant field is zero there, not strongest.

quiz.stem: How is the magnetic field between the poles of a horseshoe magnet described?
options: It is almost uniform between the poles, except near the edges
It is strongest only outside the gap
It has no field between the poles
It changes direction at every point in the gap
rationales: This is correct because the field is almost uniform between the poles except near the edges.
This is incorrect because the textbook describes the field in the gap as almost uniform.
This is incorrect because field lines cross the gap between the poles.
This is incorrect because a uniform field does not change direction at every point in the gap.

quiz.stem: Why do iron filings arrange themselves around a bar magnet in a field pattern?
options: The compass needle becomes a permanent magnet
Iron filings become tiny magnets by magnetic induction
The glass plate becomes magnetic
The filings melt and form lines
rationales: This is incorrect because the experiment explains the pattern by the filings becoming tiny magnets.
This is correct because magnetic induction makes the iron filings tiny magnets that form a pattern when the glass is tapped.
This is incorrect because the glass plate is used to hold the filings and is not said to become magnetic.
This is incorrect because the filings do not melt; they arrange into a pattern.

quiz.stem: In an A.C. generator, why is an emf induced when a coil is rotated between the poles of a permanent magnet?
options: The magnetic field through the coil changes
The coil becomes a permanent magnet
The coil stops rotating
The magnet loses all its poles
rationales: Correct: rotation changes the magnetic field through the coil, inducing an emf.
Incorrect: the coil does not need to become a permanent magnet to generate an emf.
Incorrect: the coil must rotate for the magnetic field through it to change.
Incorrect: the permanent magnet’s poles do not disappear during normal generator operation.

quiz.stem: What type of current flows through an external circuit connected to the rotating coil of an A.C. generator?
options: A.C. flows in the external circuit
Only D.C. flows in the external circuit
No current flows
The circuit becomes a permanent magnet
rationales: Correct: the induced current is alternating current when the coil ends are connected to an external circuit.
Incorrect: the section describes alternating current, not only direct current.
Incorrect: a current flows when the coil ends are connected to an external circuit.
Incorrect: connecting a generator does not turn the circuit into a permanent magnet.

quiz.stem: Which arrangement is used in the moving-coil loudspeaker described in this section?
options: A voice coil in the gap of a permanent magnet
A steel bar placed inside a refrigerator
A compass needle beside a loudspeaker
A permanent magnet attached to a microphone cone
rationales: Correct: the voice coil is inserted in the gap of the permanent magnet and attached to the cone.
Incorrect: a steel bar in a refrigerator is not the loudspeaker arrangement described.
Incorrect: a compass needle is not the part that produces the speaker’s sound.
Incorrect: the voice coil is attached to the cone, not the permanent magnet.

quiz.stem: How does a moving-coil loudspeaker produce sound in the air?
options: The cone vibrates back and forth
The cone stays still while the magnet rotates
The microphone cone attracts iron nails
The permanent magnet produces sound by itself
rationales: Correct: the varying force moves the voice coil and cone back and forth, producing sound.
Incorrect: the cone moves; the section does not describe a rotating magnet.
Incorrect: attracting iron nails is not the speaker’s sound-producing action.
Incorrect: the magnet alone does not produce the sound described.

quiz.stem: What is the purpose of the magnetic strips fitted to refrigerator and freezer doors?
options: To keep the refrigerator door closed tightly
To make the refrigerator colder by itself
To remove all the air from the refrigerator
To generate alternating current for the refrigerator
rationales: Correct: the strips help keep the doors closed tightly.
Incorrect: the strips do not cool the refrigerator.
Incorrect: the strips do not remove air from the refrigerator.
Incorrect: the strips are door seals, not generators.

quiz.stem: Why do flourmills use permanent magnets before grinding grains?
options: To remove iron nails from grains before grinding
To turn grains into iron
To make the flour magnetic
To grind the grains without a mill
rationales: Correct: the magnets remove iron objects such as nails from the grains.
Incorrect: a magnet does not turn grains into iron.
Incorrect: the purpose is to remove iron objects, not make flour magnetic.
Incorrect: magnets do not replace the grinding process.

quiz.stem: An iron nail is placed inside a coil connected to a battery. What happens when current flows?
options: It becomes a magnet only while current passes through the coil.
It remains a magnet permanently after the current stops.
It becomes magnetic only when the switch is off.
It cannot attract iron objects.
rationales: Correct: current through the coil magnetizes the iron nail, which acts as a temporary magnet.
Incorrect: the section says the iron object no longer remains a magnet when current stops.
Incorrect: the nail becomes magnetized when current passes, not when the switch is off.
Incorrect: the magnetized nail can attract objects such as paper clips.

quiz.stem: What happens to an electromagnet's iron core when the current is stopped?
options: The nail becomes a permanent magnet.
The nail no longer remains a magnet.
The coil stops having any wire turns.
The battery changes into a magnet.
rationales: Incorrect: the section describes the iron object as remaining a magnet only while current passes.
Correct: when the current is stopped, the iron object no longer remains a magnet.
Incorrect: switching off current does not change the number of turns of wire.
Incorrect: the battery is not described as becoming a magnet.

quiz.stem: Which change can increase the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Increase the number of cells or the number of coil turns.
Reduce the number of cells and coil turns.
Remove the iron core and switch off the current.
Use fewer turns and a lower current.
rationales: Correct: increasing the number of cells or coil turns increases the magnetic field strength.
Incorrect: reducing cells and turns does not produce the increase described in the section.
Incorrect: removing the core and switching off current would not strengthen this electromagnet.
Incorrect: fewer turns and lower current are not the changes given for increasing strength.

quiz.stem: How does a magnetic relay use an electromagnet?
options: A low-current input circuit activates a high-current circuit.
A high-current input circuit activates a low-current circuit.
It permanently joins two circuits with no electromagnet.
It stops all current whenever the switch is turned on.
rationales: Correct: the low-current input circuit activates another circuit that works with a high current.
Incorrect: this reverses the relay's described input and output circuits.
Incorrect: a relay works with an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature.
Incorrect: turning the relay on makes the contacts join and turns on the high-current circuit.

quiz.stem: What does a circuit breaker's electromagnet do when the current becomes excessive?
options: It attracts the armature so that it detaches from the copper strip.
It increases the current without limit.
It makes the copper strip melt intentionally.
It keeps the circuit switched on.
rationales: Correct: a sufficiently large current makes the electromagnet attract the armature away from the copper strip, breaking the circuit.
Incorrect: the circuit breaker is designed to switch the circuit off if the current is excessive.
Incorrect: the described action is the armature detaching from the copper strip, not the strip melting.
Incorrect: the circuit breaker switches off the circuit to protect appliances.

quiz.stem: How does an electromagnet help a telephone receiver produce sound?
options: The diaphragm moves back and forth as the electromagnet's force varies.
The diaphragm stays fixed and blocks all sound.
The receiver uses a permanent magnet to switch off the microphone.
The diaphragm moves only when the current is constant.
rationales: Correct: varying current changes the electromagnet's force, making the diaphragm move back and forth to produce sound.
Incorrect: the section says the diaphragm moves back and forth.
Incorrect: the described receiver uses an electromagnet and a varying current.
Incorrect: it is varying current that changes the electromagnet's force and moves the diaphragm.

quiz.stem: Which description best fits an atom that behaves as a magnetic dipole?
options: The atoms have no resultant magnetic field.
The atoms have a resultant magnetic field and act as tiny magnets.
The domains are always randomly oriented.
The material cannot contain electrons.
rationales: This describes an atom whose orbital and spin fields cancel, not a magnetic dipole.
Correct: an atom with a resultant magnetic field behaves like a tiny magnet called a magnetic dipole.
Random domain orientations describe an unmagnetized ferromagnetic piece, not one atom acting as a dipole.
All these materials contain electrons; their motions help produce magnetic fields.

quiz.stem: Which material listed in the section is paramagnetic?
options: Copper
Water
Aluminium
Bismuth
rationales: Copper is given as a diamagnetic material.
Water is given as a diamagnetic material.
Correct: aluminium is given as an example of a paramagnetic material.
Bismuth is given as a diamagnetic material.

quiz.stem: What feature of ferromagnetic materials is described in the section?
options: Their orbital and spin fields add up to zero.
Their electron spins are naturally aligned parallel in large groups of neighbouring atoms.
They have no electrons in their atoms.
Their domains are permanently random.
rationales: This describes the case where an atom has no resultant field, associated with diamagnetic materials.
Correct: large groups of neighbouring atoms have electron spins naturally aligned parallel to each other.
Atoms in these materials do have electrons, whose spins are important to their magnetism.
Ferromagnetic domains can become aligned; they are not necessarily permanently random.

quiz.stem: Which statement about a magnetic domain is correct?
options: Each domain acts as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.
Each domain is a single electron.
Each domain is an unmagnetized piece with no poles.
Each domain is a region that blocks an external magnetic field.
rationales: Correct: each domain behaves as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.
A domain is a region containing a large group of atoms, not a single electron.
A domain is highly magnetized, so it is not described as having no poles.
The section describes domains as aligning in an external field, not blocking it.

quiz.stem: What happens when an external magnetic field is applied to an unmagnetized piece of iron?
options: The domains shrink and become random.
Domains aligned with the field grow, while other domains rotate towards the field.
All domains disappear.
The domains become aligned opposite to the external field.
rationales: The section says the domains become more aligned, not that they all become random.
Correct: aligned or nearly aligned domains grow, and other domains rotate towards the external field.
Domains do not disappear; their size and alignment change.
The domains become oriented in the direction of the external field, not opposite to it.

quiz.stem: Which material has domains that are easily oriented by an external field and return to random positions when the field is removed?
options: Soft iron
Steel
Copper
Nickel
rationales: Correct: the section says domains in soft iron are easily oriented and return to random positions when the field is removed.
Steel retains its domain alignment and is used to make permanent magnets.
Copper is non-ferromagnetic and does not form magnetic domains as described.
Nickel is ferromagnetic, but the section specifically describes soft iron as having domains that readily return to random positions.

quiz.stem: Why does an unmagnetized piece of iron not display magnetism?
options: The magnetic effects of the domains cancel each other.
The iron has no domains.
Every domain points in the same direction.
The iron changes into a diamagnetic material.
rationales: Correct: randomly oriented domains have magnetic fields that cancel each other.
The section states that ferromagnetic materials contain domains.
In an unmagnetized piece, domains are randomly oriented, not all pointing the same way.
Iron remains ferromagnetic; it is the domain orientations that explain its unmagnetized state.

quiz.stem: Which procedure describes the single-touch method of magnetising a steel bar?
options: Stroke it repeatedly in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the end of each stroke.
Stroke it back and forth with alternating poles without lifting the magnet.
Heat it strongly while stroking it.
Place it in a solenoid carrying alternating current.
rationales: This is correct: single-touch uses the same pole in the same direction, with the magnet lifted at the end of each stroke.
This is incorrect because single-touch does not use alternating poles or back-and-forth strokes.
This is incorrect because strong heating demagnetises a magnet rather than being part of single-touch magnetising.
This is incorrect because the section uses direct current in a solenoid to magnetise the bar; A.C. is used for demagnetisation.

quiz.stem: What is done in the double-touch method of magnetising a steel bar?
options: It uses unlike poles of two magnets stroking outwards from the centre at the same time.
It uses one magnet stroking from the centre towards one end only.
It uses like poles of two magnets stroking towards the centre.
It uses a solenoid carrying alternating current.
rationales: This is correct: double-touch uses unlike poles and strokes outwards from the centre simultaneously.
This is incorrect because the method uses two magnets and strokes towards both ends.
This is incorrect because the poles used are unlike, and the strokes move outwards from the centre.
This is incorrect because double-touch is a stroking method, not the A.C. solenoid method.

quiz.stem: After stroking, what is the polarity of the poles produced at the ends of the steel bar?
options: The ends have polarity opposite to that of the stroking pole.
The ends have the same polarity as the stroking pole.
Both ends always become north poles.
The ends remain unmagnetised.
rationales: This is correct: the section states that each end has polarity opposite to the stroking pole.
This is incorrect because the section says the polarity is opposite, not the same.
This is incorrect because the two ends of a magnet have opposite polarities.
This is incorrect because stroking induces magnetism in the steel bar.

quiz.stem: Which current is passed through the solenoid to magnetise the steel bar?
options: Direct current
Alternating current
No current
A current that repeatedly stops and starts in one direction only
rationales: This is correct: the section says direct current through the solenoid magnetises the steel bar.
This is incorrect because alternating current in a solenoid is described as a way to demagnetise a magnet.
This is incorrect because a current is needed to magnetise the bar by this method.
This is incorrect because the method specifies direct current, not an intermittent current.

quiz.stem: How is the right-hand grip rule used to find the polarity of a bar inside a current-carrying solenoid?
options: Curl the right-hand fingers in the direction of current; the thumb points to the N-pole end.
Curl the left-hand fingers in the direction of current; the thumb points to the S-pole end.
Point the right-hand thumb in the direction of current; the fingers show the N-pole end.
Curl the right-hand fingers opposite to the current; the thumb points to the S-pole end.
rationales: This is correct: the right-hand fingers follow the current, and the thumb points towards the N-pole end.
This is incorrect because the rule uses the right hand and the thumb points to the N-pole end.
This is incorrect because the fingers curl along the current and the thumb identifies the N-pole end.
This is incorrect because the fingers curl along, not opposite to, the current, and the thumb points to the N-pole end.

quiz.stem: Which action is described as a way to demagnetise a magnet?
options: Strong heating
Cooling it gently
Placing it in a solenoid carrying direct current
Stroking it repeatedly in one direction
rationales: This is correct: strong heating causes thermal vibrations that disturb the order of the domains.
This is incorrect because gentle cooling is not given as a demagnetising method in the section.
This is incorrect because direct current in a solenoid is used to magnetise a steel bar.
This is incorrect because stroking in one direction is used to magnetise a steel bar.

quiz.stem: Why can hammering demagnetise a magnet?
options: Beating it disturbs the alignment of its domains.
It makes the domains align more strongly.
It changes the magnet into a solenoid.
It increases the current inside the magnet.
rationales: This is correct: the section says that beating a magnet makes its domains lose their alignment.
This is incorrect because hammering disrupts domain alignment rather than strengthening it.
This is incorrect because hammering does not turn a magnet into a coil of wire.
This is incorrect because a permanent magnet does not have an electric current inside it in this explanation.

quiz.stem: How is a magnet demagnetised using a solenoid carrying alternating current?
options: Move the magnet out slowly from inside the solenoid.
Move the magnet into the solenoid quickly and leave it there.
Pass direct current through the solenoid and keep the magnet inside.
Heat the solenoid while the magnet is inside it.
rationales: This is correct: the section describes slowly moving a magnet out from inside an A.C.-carrying solenoid.
This is incorrect because the described method requires slowly moving the magnet out, not quickly moving it in.
This is incorrect because direct current in a solenoid is used to magnetise steel.
This is incorrect because heating the solenoid is not the stated A.C. demagnetisation method.

quiz.stem: What is a magnetic tape recording head made of, according to this section?
options: A coil of wire wrapped around an iron core
A permanent magnet with no coil
A plastic block with a metal coating
A compass needle
rationales: This is correct: the recording and playing head is a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core.
This is wrong: the section describes an electromagnet, not a permanent magnet alone.
This is wrong: the head has an iron core and coil, not a plastic block with a metal coating.
This is wrong: a compass needle is not the recording head described.

quiz.stem: Which part of the recording head’s magnetic field penetrates the tape coating?
options: The straight field lines outside the head
The curved part of the magnetic field in the gap
The current flowing through the tape
The plastic backing of the tape
rationales: This is wrong: the section identifies the curved part of the field in the gap.
This is correct: the curved part is called the fringe field and penetrates the magnetic coating.
This is wrong: current is sent to the head, not through the tape.
This is wrong: the plastic backing supports the tape but does not record the signal.

quiz.stem: What happens to the tape’s magnetic coating after it leaves the recording head?
options: It becomes permanently non-magnetic
It retains induced magnetism after leaving the recording head
It turns into an electrical signal immediately
Its plastic backing stores the magnetic pattern
rationales: This is wrong: the section says the induced magnetism is retained.
This is correct: the induced magnetism remains when the tape leaves the vicinity of the head.
This is wrong: the stored magnetic pattern is later converted back into varying current during playback.
This is wrong: the magnetic coating, not the plastic backing, stores the pattern.

quiz.stem: How does a hard-disk magnetic head write a binary digit?
options: By magnetising tiny spots in different directions
By cutting grooves into the disk
By storing sound as heat
By changing the disk’s size
rationales: This is correct: the head writes 1 or 0 by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
This is wrong: the section describes magnetic recording, not grooves cut into the disk.
This is wrong: the information is stored magnetically, not as heat.
This is wrong: changing the disk’s size is not how the head records a digit.

quiz.stem: What coating does the section say is used on hard disks?
options: The disk is coated on both sides with iron oxide
The disk is made only of iron
The disk is coated with plastic backing
The disk contains a moving tape
rationales: This is correct: hard disks are coated on both sides with iron oxide.
This is wrong: the disk may be made of aluminium, glass or plastic, with an iron oxide coating.
This is wrong: plastic backing is described as part of a tape, not a hard-disk coating.
This is wrong: a hard disk is a circular plate and does not contain a moving tape.

quiz.stem: What advantage of magnetic disks over tape recorders is given in this section?
options: A disk can read or write a recording instantly
A disk needs many minutes to locate information
A tape can store only binary digits
A disk does not need a magnetic head
rationales: This is correct: a disk unit can read or write a recording instantly.
This is wrong: the section says locating information on tape may take many minutes.
This is wrong: the section does not say that tape stores only binary digits.
This is wrong: the section describes a magnetic head for reading and writing a disk.

quiz.stem: Which material does the section recommend for boxes that protect electronic devices from strong magnetic effects?
options: Soft iron
Wood
Plastic
Glass
rationales: This is correct: the section says to enclose devices in boxes made of soft iron.
This is wrong: wood is not the material recommended in the section.
This is wrong: plastic is not the material recommended in the section.
This is wrong: glass is not the material recommended in the section.

quiz.stem: Why does a soft iron casing help shield a sensitive magnetic device from an external magnetic field?
options: Because soft iron has higher magnetic permeability than air
Because soft iron blocks every magnetic field completely
Because soft iron is a permanent magnet
Because the device inside produces no magnetic field
rationales: Correct: magnetic flux is established more readily in the high-permeability soft iron than in air or the device.
Incorrect: the textbook explains that flux is established in the soft iron, not that the field is completely blocked.
Incorrect: the shielding explanation depends on permeability, not on soft iron acting as a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: shielding works because of the casing's effect on magnetic flux, not because the device produces no field.

quiz.stem: When a sensitive device is enclosed in a soft iron casing, where is the magnetic flux established mainly?
options: Magnetic flux is established mainly in the soft iron casing
Magnetic flux is forced to pass through the sensitive device
The casing changes the external field into an electric current
The soft iron casing removes the magnetic poles of the external magnets
rationales: Correct: the flux is established in the soft iron rather than in the device.
Incorrect: the casing helps keep the flux from being established in the sensitive device.
Incorrect: the section describes magnetic flux and shielding, not conversion into electric current.
Incorrect: the casing does not remove the poles of the magnets producing the external field.

quiz.stem: Which property of soft iron is most important for its use as a magnetic shield?
options: High magnetic permeability
High electrical resistance
A permanent north pole
A high melting point
rationales: Correct: high permeability allows magnetic flux to pass through the soft iron readily.
Incorrect: electrical resistance is not the property described as causing magnetic shielding.
Incorrect: soft iron is used for its permeability, not because it has a permanent north pole.
Incorrect: melting point is not given as the reason for its shielding use.

quiz.stem: Why is a soft iron shielding casing usually made with rounded corners?
options: Rounded corners help magnetic field lines line up easily
Rounded corners increase the electrical current in the device
Rounded corners make soft iron a permanent magnet
Rounded corners stop all magnetic flux from entering the casing
rationales: Correct: rounded corners facilitate the magnetic field lines lining up easily.
Incorrect: the shape of the casing is not described as increasing current in the device.
Incorrect: rounded corners do not make soft iron a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: the casing provides an easier path for flux; it does not stop all flux from entering it.

quiz.stem: Why is soft iron suitable for the core of an electromagnet?
options: It is easily magnetised when current flows and quickly loses magnetism when current stops
It remains permanently magnetised after current stops
It has lower permeability than air
It cannot be magnetised by a magnetic field
rationales: Correct: soft iron is easily magnetised by the current and quickly loses its magnetism when the current stops.
Incorrect: a core that stays magnetised permanently would not match the temporary action described for an electromagnet.
Incorrect: soft iron has high permeability, not lower permeability than air.
Incorrect: soft iron can be magnetised when current passes around it.

quiz.stem: What is one effect of placing a soft iron core inside a moving coil galvanometer?
options: The sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is increased
The galvanometer becomes a permanent magnet
The external magnetic field is eliminated
The coil no longer carries current
rationales: Correct: the section states that a soft iron core increases the galvanometer's sensitivity.
Incorrect: the stated effect is increased sensitivity, not making the galvanometer a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: the core does not eliminate every external magnetic field.
Incorrect: adding a core does not stop the coil from carrying current.

quiz.stem: Which use of soft iron is stated in this section?
options: It is used in the core of an electromagnet
It is used to make an electromagnet retain magnetism forever
It prevents current from flowing in the coil
It is used because its permeability is lower than air
rationales: Correct: the section says soft iron is generally used in the cores of electromagnets.
Incorrect: soft iron quickly loses magnetism when the current is stopped, rather than retaining it forever.
Incorrect: the core does not prevent current from flowing in the surrounding coil.
Incorrect: soft iron has higher, not lower, permeability than air.

quiz.stem: Which arrangement is described as protecting a sensitive magnetic device from an external magnetic field?
options: A sensitive magnetic device enclosed in a soft iron casing
A permanent magnet placed beside the device
A wooden casing around the device
A steel bar placed far from the device
rationales: Correct: the section describes enclosing the sensitive device in a soft iron casing.
Incorrect: placing a permanent magnet beside the device is not the shielding method described.
Incorrect: the section identifies soft iron, not wood, as the shielding material.
Incorrect: a steel bar placed far away is not the stated shielding arrangement.

quiz.stem: Q8.1. Which one of the following is not a magnetic material?
options: Cobalt
Iron
Aluminium
Nickel
rationales: Cobalt is a magnetic material.
Iron is a magnetic material.
Aluminium is not a ferromagnetic material like iron, cobalt and nickel, so this is the intended answer.
Nickel is a magnetic material.

quiz.stem: Q8.2. Magnetic lines of force:
options: are always directed in a straight line
cross one another
enter into the north pole
enter into the south pole
rationales: Magnetic field lines are generally curved outside a magnet, not always straight.
Magnetic field lines never cross because the field cannot have two directions at one point.
Outside a magnet, field lines emerge from the north pole rather than entering it.
Outside a magnet, field lines enter the south pole.

quiz.stem: Q8.3. Permanent magnets cannot be made by:
options: soft iron
steel
neodymium
alnico
rationales: Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it is unsuitable for permanent magnets.
Steel can retain magnetism and can be used to make permanent magnets.
Neodymium is used to make strong permanent magnets.
Alnico is an alloy used to make permanent magnets.

quiz.stem: Q8.4. Permanent magnets are used in:
options: circuit breaker
loudspeaker
electric crane
magnetic recording
rationales: A circuit breaker commonly uses an electromagnet so that the magnetic effect can respond to current.
A loudspeaker commonly uses a permanent magnet interacting with a current-carrying coil.
An electric crane uses an electromagnet that can be switched on and off.
Magnetic recording uses magnetic materials and a recording magnetic field rather than relying on the listed permanent-magnet application.

quiz.stem: Q8.5. A common method used to magnetise a material is:
options: stroking
hitting
heating
placing inside a solenoid having A.C
rationales: Stroking a magnetic material with a magnet is a common magnetising method.
Hitting is not the standard method for magnetising a material.
Heating generally weakens or destroys magnetism rather than magnetising the material.
Alternating current in a solenoid is commonly used to demagnetise a material.

quiz.stem: Q8.7. A steel rod is magnetised by double touch stroking method. Which one would be the correct polarity of the AB magnet?
rationales: With the described opposite poles stroking outwards from the centre, the left end becomes N and the right end becomes S.
This reverses the polarity expected from the indicated stroking arrangement.
The bar is magnetised with one north pole at each end, which is not the resulting polarity.
The bar is magnetised with one south pole at each end, which is not the resulting polarity.

quiz.stem: Q8.8. The best material to protect a device from external magnetic field is:
options: wood
plastic
steel
soft iron
rationales: Wood is not an effective magnetic shield.
Plastic is not an effective magnetic shield.
Steel is not the best choice here for shielding the device.
Soft iron provides an easy path for magnetic field lines and is used for magnetic shielding.

written.text: How can you identify whether an object is a magnet or a magnetic material?
modelAnswer: Bring the object close to a known magnet.
If the object repels the magnet, the object is a magnet.
If the object is attracted but does not repel, it is a magnetic material, not a magnet.

rubric.why: A known magnet is needed to carry out the test.
rubric.how: Bring the object close to a known magnet.

rubric.description: Explain that repulsion shows the object is a magnet.
rubric.why: Repulsion distinguishes a magnet from an ordinary magnetic material.

written.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with reference to the domain theory.
